query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of titanium to a refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g. NbMoTaW or NbMoTaWV) will improve the strength–plasticity combination by enhancing grain boundary cohesion.
generation.material_initial_state: A typical refractory high‐entropy alloy (such as NbMoTaW or NbMoTaWV) produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, which exhibits very high strength but limited plasticity (i.e. brittle behavior at room temperature).
generation.intervention: Introduce a modest Ti addition into the alloy’s composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tested under identical processing (e.g., mechanical alloying and SPS) and mechanical testing conditions at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Improved grain boundary chemistry and cohesion, with subtle segregation or solid solution effects that reduce intergranular brittleness.
generation.mechanism: Titanium is expected to modify the grain boundary structure by reducing boundary energy and enhancing cohesion. This change can delay crack initiation and propagation while allowing dislocation activity and promoting a more ductile failure mode, all without severely compromising the inherent high strength provided by the refractory elements.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-modified alloy should display a noticeable increase in plastic strain (improvements on the order of ~10% absolute strain increase, for example achieving ductilities such as 11.5% versus lower values in the base alloy) while keeping yield strength close to or within a modest decrement of the unmodified alloy’s performance.
generation.baseline: The unmodified refractory HEA, which exhibits high yield strength but is brittle with very low plasticity at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a limited Ti concentration range. Excess Ti might lead to unwanted phase formation or embrittlement, so the intervention is effective only if the Ti content is optimized to enhance grain boundary cohesion without introducing deleterious Ti-rich phases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact concentration of Ti needed for the optimal balance and the magnitude of the improvement in plasticity remain to be experimentally determined; variations in processing route or alloy system nuances may also affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one with the standard refractory HEA composition (e.g., NbMoTaW or NbMoTaWV) and one with an optimized, modest Ti addition. Process both using identical mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering parameters. Characterize microstructure (via TEM, SEM, and XRD) to ensure phase consistency and analyze grain boundary features. Perform tensile and compression tests at room and elevated temperatures to compare yield strength, ductility, and overall toughness.
measurements: Phase purity and detection of potential secondary phases (via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement in plasticity (e.g., a less than ~5–10% increase in plastic strain) without a meaningful drop in yield strength compared to the baseline alloy, or if detrimental Ti-rich phases appear, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa []. Multi-component refractory elements-based alloys possess a mainly BCC structure. One of the most interesting HEA types is a system with coherent BCC and B2 phases with a microstructure similar to Ni-based alloys. The difference is that the disordered BCC phase is present as cubic nanoparticles. This structure provides a combination of high strength and high plasticity at high temperatures and is standard for Al-containing multi-component alloys. Thus, for the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy, its yield strength is 745 MPa at 1000 °C, and good plasticity is preserved (the height decrease is >50% under compression) []. However, there can also be observed oxides and intermetallic phases, such as Laves phases, in the refractory HEAs that can affect the materials’ ductility. For example, in the NbCrMoTaTiZr, CrNbTiZr, and CrNbTiVZr alloys, the Laves phase is formed in the BCC-matrix because of the smaller radius of Cr in comparison to other elements [,,]. Nevertheless, in Reference [], an NbMoTaWVCr alloy with an extremely high yield strength of 3416 MPa and good plasticity of 5.3% at room temperature was obtained.
